claim: Recent work has demonstrated the accuracy of coevolution-based contact prediction for monomeric proteins using a global statistical model to distinguish between direct and indirect couplings.
source: Recent work has demonstrated the accuracy of coevolution-based contact prediction for monomeric proteins using a global statistical model (Thomas et al., 2008) to distinguish between direct and indirect couplings (Marks et al., 2011; Morcos et al., 2011; Hopf et al., 2012; Nugent and Jones, 2012; Jones et al., 2012; Lapedes et al., 2012; Marks et al., 2012; Sułkowska et al., 2012; Kamisetty et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior work demonstrating coevolution-based contact prediction accuracy.

claim: Early approaches to coevolution-based contact prediction relied on estimating an inverse covariance matrix.
source: While early approaches relied on estimating an inverse covariance matrix (Marks et al., 2011; Morcos et al., 2011; Jones et al., 2012), more recent studies have shown that a pseudo-likelihood-based approach (Balakrishnan et al., 2011) results in more accurate predictions (Ekeberg et al., 2013; Kamisetty et al., 2013) for a range of alignment sizes and protein lengths.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work using inverse covariance matrix approaches.

claim: A pseudo-likelihood-based approach results in more accurate predictions than inverse covariance matrix methods for a range of alignment sizes and protein lengths.
source: While early approaches relied on estimating an inverse covariance matrix (Marks et al., 2011; Morcos et al., 2011; Jones et al., 2012), more recent studies have shown that a pseudo-likelihood-based approach (Balakrishnan et al., 2011) results in more accurate predictions (Ekeberg et al., 2013; Kamisetty et al., 2013) for a range of alignment sizes and protein lengths.
evidence: Supported by citations to studies comparing pseudo-likelihood and inverse covariance approaches.

claim: Relatively little is known about the utility of global statistical models in predicting protein–protein interactions compared to monomeric proteins.
source: In contrast to this rich body of work for monomeric proteins, relatively little is known about the utility of such statistical models in predicting protein–protein interactions.
evidence: This is a comparative statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The problem of predicting if two proteins interact with each other has been studied extensively using a wide variety of approaches.
source: The more general problem of predicting if two proteins interact with each other has been studied extensively using a wide variety of approaches (de Juan et al., 2013; Hosur et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2012; Shoemaker and Panchenko, 2007, Valencia and Pazos, 2002, Ochoa and Pazos, 2010).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior work on protein interaction prediction.

claim: Amino acid residue coevolution has been used to predict residue–residue interactions across interfaces with local statistical models.
source: Amino acid residue coevolution has been used to predict residue–residue interactions across interfaces with local statistical models (Pazos et al., 1997; Halperin et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work using local statistical models.

claim: The accuracy of local statistical models is reduced by the confounding of direct and indirect correlations.
source: As noted above, the accuracy of these models is reduced by the confounding of direct and indirect correlations (Lapedes et al., 1999; Weigt et al., 2009)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work discussing limitations of local models.

claim: The application of global statistical models to coevolution-based contact prediction across interfaces has been limited to the histidine-kinase/response-regulator two component system.
source: the application of global statistical models to coevolution-based contact prediction across interfaces has been limited to the case of the histidine-kinase/response-regulator two component system (Burger and van Nimwegen, 2008; Weigt et al., 2009; Schug et al., 2009; Dago et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work on this specific system.

claim: Covarying pairs of positions are almost always in contact in the three-dimensional structure of protein complexes, provided there are sufficient aligned sequences.
source: In a large set of complexes of known structure, we find that covarying pairs of positions are almost always in contact in the three-dimensional structure, provided there are sufficient aligned sequences.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on analysis of known structures.

claim: Significant residue–residue covariance occurs frequently between physically interacting protein pairs but very rarely between non-interacting pairs.
source: We find further that significant residue–residue covariance occurs frequently between physically interacting protein pairs but very rarely between non-interacting pairs, and hence should be useful for predicting whether two proteins interact.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis of protein pairs.

claim: In the 50S ribosomal subunit, only a small fraction of residue pairs coevolve, as indicated by coupling strengths greater than 1.5.
source: We find that in the 50S ribosomal subunit only a small fraction of residue pairs coevolve, as indicated by coupling strengths (y axis of Figure 1A) greater than 1.5.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis of the 50S ribosome, with reference to Figure 1A.

claim: Residue pairs with coupling strengths greater than 1.5 in the 50S ribosomal subunit are almost all within 8 Å of each other in the crystal structure.
source: Remarkably, the two residues in each of these pairs are almost all within 8 Å of each other in the 50S crystal structure (Figure 1A) and all are within 12 Å.
evidence: This is a finding from comparing coupling strengths to distances in the crystal structure, shown in Figure 1A.

claim: All residue pairs with coupling strengths greater than 1.5 in the 50S ribosomal subunit are within 12 Å of each other in the crystal structure.
source: Remarkably, the two residues in each of these pairs are almost all within 8 Å of each other in the 50S crystal structure (Figure 1A) and all are within 12 Å.
evidence: This is a finding from comparing coupling strengths to distances in the crystal structure.

claim: For the 50S ribosome, the GREMLIN model was built using sequence data from approximately 1500 non-redundant genomes.
source: For the 50S ribosome, the GREMLIN model was built using sequence data from ∼1500 non-redundant genomes
evidence: This describes the data used in the analysis.

claim: For complexes with large numbers of aligned sequences (like the 50S ribosome), residue–residue interactions across interfaces can be predicted with quite high confidence based on amino acid sequence covariation.
source: Figure 1D suggests that for complexes with such large numbers of aligned sequence, residue–residue interactions across interfaces can be predicted with quite high confidence based on amino acid sequence covariation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The greater the number of aligned sequences, the lower the value of the coupling strength above which residue pairs are likely to be in contact in the structure.
source: We find that the greater the number of aligned sequences, the lower the value of the coupling strength above which residue pairs are likely to be in contact in the structure (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of sub-alignments with varying sequence depths, shown in Figure 1D.

claim: If the number of aligned sequences is greater than the sum of the lengths of the two proteins, residue–residue contact predictions are likely to be accurate if the coupling strength is 2 or greater.
source: For example, if the number of aligned sequences is greater than the sum of the lengths of the two proteins, residue–residue contact predictions are likely to be accurate if the coupling strength is 2 or greater (Figure 1D: orange dots)
evidence: This is a specific finding from the analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: If there are twice as many sequences as the sum of protein lengths, contact predictions are accurate above a coupling strength of 1.5.
source: while if there are twice as many sequences, contact predictions are accurate above a coupling strength of 1.5 (the cutoff shown in Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a specific finding from the analysis.

claim: In the 50S subunit, every pair of proteins with summed coupling strengths greater than 1.5 interacts with each other.
source: In the 50S subunit, every pair of proteins with summed coupling strengths (numbers in Figure 1C) greater than 1.5 interacts with each other (boxes in Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of protein-protein interactions in the 50S subunit, shown in Figure 1C.

claim: There are several instances of protein pairs that contact in the 50S subunit for which no covariance is observed.
source: There are, however, several instances of protein pairs that contact in the 50S subunit for which no covariance is observed
evidence: This is an observation from the analysis of the 50S subunit.

claim: Not every interaction will be identified by the sum of the coupling strengths, for example between two proteins that are held together primarily by the ribosomal RNA.
source: clearly not every interaction will be identified by the sum of the coupling strengths, for example between two proteins that are held together primarily by the ribosomal RNA.
evidence: This is an interpretation of why some interactions are not detected.

claim: 1126 E. coli gene pairs had paired alignments with at least as many sequences as the average of the lengths of the two proteins.
source: As the 50S results (Figure 1D) suggested that alignment depths greater than the average of the lengths of the two proteins were required for accurate prediction, we focused on paired alignments with at least this number of sequences—1126 gene pairs in total excluding the ribosomal proteins.
evidence: This describes the dataset used in the analysis.

claim: For 64 of the 1126 gene pairs, at least one pair of residues had GREMLIN score >0.85.
source: For 64 of the 1126 gene pairs, at least one pair of residues had GREMLIN score >0.85.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of E. coli gene pairs.

claim: For 28 of the 64 gene pairs with high GREMLIN scores, three-dimensional structures have been determined experimentally.
source: For 28 of the 64 pairs three-dimensional structures have been determined experimentally
evidence: This describes the availability of structural data for validation.

claim: Almost all pairs with GREMLIN scores greater than 0.6 are in contact in the complex structures, with the notable exception of the NADH dehydrogenase subunits.
source: Almost all pairs with GREMLIN scores greater than 0.6 are in contact in the complex structures, with the notable exception of the NADH dehydrogenase subunits (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a finding from comparing predicted contacts to known structures, with reference to Figure 2B.

claim: The NADH dehydrogenase complex is thought to undergo a cascade of conformational changes during electron transfer.
source: The complex is thought to undergo a cascade of conformational changes during electron transfer (Baradaran et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work on NADH dehydrogenase.

claim: The high GREMLIN score contacts not made in the solved structure of NADH dehydrogenase may provide insight into the nature of conformational changes.
source: the high GREMLIN score contacts not made in the solved structure may provide insight into the nature of these changes.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the discrepancy between predictions and structure.

claim: 44% (28/64) of the protein pairs with high GREMLIN scores form a complex which has been solved crystallographically.
source: 44% (28/64) of the protein pairs with high GREMLIN scores form a complex which has been solved crystallographically compared to 8% (78/1126) over the whole set.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the analysis.

claim: 8% (78/1126) of all E. coli gene pairs in the dataset form a complex which has been solved crystallographically.
source: 44% (28/64) of the protein pairs with high GREMLIN scores form a complex which has been solved crystallographically compared to 8% (78/1126) over the whole set.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the analysis.

claim: The existence of one or more high GREMLIN scores between two proteins provides evidence that the proteins interact.
source: As observed for the 50S complex (Figure 1C), the existence of one or more high GREMLIN scores between two proteins provides evidence that the proteins interact
evidence: This is an inference from the data comparing high GREMLIN scores to known interactions.

claim: Interactions can be accurately predicted across protein–protein interfaces given a sufficient number of aligned sequences.
source: The results with the 50S ribosome and the protein pairs in the benchmark suggest that interactions can be accurately predicted across protein–protein interfaces given a sufficient number of aligned sequences.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the results with the 50S ribosome and benchmark set.

claim: The docking protocol generated models with interface RMSD within 4 Å of the native interface in 14 of 18 test cases.
source: The model with the best restraint score had an interface that was within 4 Å (in root mean square deviation) of the native interface in 14 of the 18 cases and had more than half the native contacts in 16 of the 18 cases (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the docking test set analysis, shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The docking protocol generated models with more than half the native contacts in 16 of 18 test cases.
source: The model with the best restraint score had an interface that was within 4 Å (in root mean square deviation) of the native interface in 14 of the 18 cases and had more than half the native contacts in 16 of the 18 cases (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the docking test set analysis, shown in Figure 4A.

claim: In the absence of conformational changes, predicted contact guided docking is very accurate.
source: In the absence of conformational changes, predicted contact guided docking is very accurate.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the docking results.

claim: The docking protocol on a positive control set of 41 protein-pairs generated models that were within 2 Å of the native complex structure in 38 cases.
source: The same protocol, on a positive control set of known bound structures of 41 protein-pairs (including 15 protein-pairs from the NADH electron transport complex), generated models that were within 2 Å of the native complex structure in 38 cases and within 4 Å in all but one case (Figure 4—source data 1, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the positive control analysis.

claim: The docking protocol on a positive control set of 41 protein-pairs generated models that were within 4 Å in all but one case.
source: The same protocol, on a positive control set of known bound structures of 41 protein-pairs (including 15 protein-pairs from the NADH electron transport complex), generated models that were within 2 Å of the native complex structure in 38 cases and within 4 Å in all but one case (Figure 4—source data 1, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the positive control analysis.

claim: In cases with small conformational change, the docking protocol can recover the entire interface to high accuracy.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that in cases with small conformational change, the docking protocol can recover the entire interface to high accuracy
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the docking results.

claim: In cases where binding is accompanied by a large conformational change, the docking protocol recovers the largest intact and/or unobstructed interface.
source: and in cases where binding is accompanied by a large conformational change, the protocol recovers the largest intact and/or unobstructed interface.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the docking results.

claim: The TRAP transporters are composed of three proteins: two integral membrane proteins YIAM and YIAN, and one periplasmic protein YIAO.
source: The tripartite ATP-independent periplasmic (TRAP) transporters are composed of three proteins: two integral membrane proteins YIAM and YIAN, and one periplasmic protein YIAO (Mulligan et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work on TRAP transporters.

claim: The structure of the periplasmic domain of TRAP transporters is known, but the membrane portion is unknown.
source: The structure of the periplasmic domain is known, but the membrane portion is unknown.
evidence: This describes the state of structural knowledge for TRAP transporters.

claim: In the TRAP complex model, YIAO interacts with both of the membrane components.
source: In the resultant model of the complex (Figure 5), YIAO interacts with both of the membrane components; this is supported by a number of intersubunit contacts (yellow lines).
evidence: This is a finding from the structural modeling, shown in Figure 5.

claim: Tripartite efflux complexes span both the inner and outer membrane.
source: Tripartite efflux complexes span both the inner and outer membrane, and are widely used in bacteria to pump toxic compounds out of the cell.
evidence: This is established knowledge about tripartite efflux systems.

claim: Tripartite efflux complexes are widely used in bacteria to pump toxic compounds out of the cell.
source: Tripartite efflux complexes span both the inner and outer membrane, and are widely used in bacteria to pump toxic compounds out of the cell.
evidence: This is established knowledge about tripartite efflux systems.

claim: The mode of interactions between the outer membrane factor and the membrane fusion protein in tripartite efflux systems is unresolved.
source: The mode of interactions between the outer membrane factor and the membrane fusion protein is unresolved, with reports suggesting either a tip-to-tip interaction, the insertion of one into the other, or a multistage interaction with an initial tip-to-tip interaction, followed by sliding one through the channel of the other (Long et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work discussing different proposed interaction modes.

claim: The predicted residue–residue contacts for tripartite efflux complexes support the tip-to-tip interaction model.
source: The predicted residue–residue contacts for this family of complexes support the tip-to-tip interaction (Figure 4; yellow lines)
evidence: This is a finding from the coevolution analysis and modeling.

claim: The coevolution data for tripartite efflux complexes did not provide any evidence to support the insertion model.
source: the coevolution data did not provide any evidence to support the insertion model.
evidence: This is a finding from the coevolution analysis.

claim: Pyruvate formate-lyase (PFL) catalyzes the reaction of acetyl-CoA and formate from pyruvate and CoA in the Fermentation pathway.
source: Pyruvate formate-lyase (PFL) catalyzes the reaction of acetyl-CoA and formate from pyruvate and CoA in the Fermentation pathway.
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge about PFL.

claim: Formate acetyltransferase 1 or Pyruvate formate-lyase 1 (PFLB) is activated by Pyruvate formate-lyase 1-activating enzyme (PFLA).
source: Formate acetyltransferase 1 or Pyruvate formate-lyase 1 (PFLB) is activated by Pyruvate formate-lyase 1-activating enzyme (PFLA).
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge about PFL activation.

claim: The structure of the PFL complex is unknown, but the structures of the individual proteins have been solved.
source: The structure of the complex is unknown, but the structures of the individual proteins have been solved (PDB ids: 3c8f [Becker and Kabsch, 2002] and 1h16 [Vey et al., 2008]).
evidence: This describes the state of structural knowledge for the PFL complex, with citations to structures of individual proteins.

claim: The region that undergoes conformational change in the activating enzyme upon substrate binding is in the region predicted to be in contact with PFL.
source: Interestingly, the region that undergoes conformational change in the activating enzyme upon substrate binding (3c8f -> 3cb8 [Becker and Kabsch, 2002]) is in the region we predict to be in contact with PFL.
evidence: This is a finding from comparing the predicted contacts to known conformational changes, with citation to structural data.

claim: There is strong selective pressure at protein–protein interfaces beyond simple residue conservation.
source: Our results demonstrate unequivocally that there is strong selective pressure at protein–protein interfaces beyond simple residue conservation
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the results of the study.

claim: Co-evolving residue pairs are nearly always in contact in the protein complex.
source: and that co-evolving residue pairs are nearly always in contact in the protein complex.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study.

claim: Not all contacting residues across protein interfaces likely co-evolve nor all protein–protein interfaces.
source: Not all contacting residues across protein interfaces likely co-evolve nor all protein–protein interfaces.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the limitations of the approach.

claim: There is sufficient coevolutionary signal to significantly constrain models of a large number of protein complexes.
source: Nevertheless, as illustrated in Figures 1 and 2, there is clearly sufficient coevolutionary signal to significantly constrain models of a large number of protein complexes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the results shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Contacts could be predicted with high accuracy for monomeric proteins, provided there were sufficient aligned sequences.
source: We found previously (Kamisetty et al., 2013) that contacts could be predicted with high accuracy for monomeric proteins, provided there were sufficient aligned sequences
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: For monomeric proteins with sufficient aligned sequences for accurate contact prediction, there was almost always already a structure of a family member from which comparative models could be built.
source: but in such cases there was almost always already a structure of a family member from which comparative models could be built, limiting the utility of the predicted contacts in structure prediction
evidence: This is an observation about the practical utility of contact prediction for monomeric proteins.

claim: More than half of the complexes for which the protein families of the constituent subunits are sufficiently large for accurate contact prediction do not currently have three-dimensional structures.
source: In contrast, here we find that more than half of the complexes for which the protein families of the constituent subunits are sufficiently large for accurate contact prediction do not currently have three-dimensional structures.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of protein complexes in the study.

claim: Predicted contacts are more useful for structure modeling for protein complexes than for monomeric proteins due to the much poorer representation of protein complexes in the PDB.
source: Hence, while predicted contacts can be very accurate for both monomeric globular proteins and for protein–protein complexes, they are more useful for structure modeling for the latter due to the much poorer representation of protein complexes in the PDB.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the utility of contact prediction for monomers vs. complexes.

claim: The current study focuses on prokaryotes and mitochondria.
source: While our approach of constructing a global statistical model from paired sequence alignments is generally applicable to any taxa, the current study focuses on prokaryotes and mitochondria.
evidence: This describes the scope of the study.

claim: The study exploits the operon architecture of bacterial genomes to largely avoid the problem of distinguishing between paralogs.
source: Doing so allows us to largely avoid the problem of distinguishing between paralogs by exploiting the operon architecture of bacterial genomes (Jacob et al., 2005).
evidence: This describes the methodological approach, with citation to prior work on operons.

claim: Constructing paired-sequence alignments for more complex genomic architectures is more involved and requires the ability to distinguish orthologs from paralogs.
source: Constructing paired-sequence alignments for more complex genomic architectures is more involved and requires the ability to distinguish orthologs from paralogs, the subject of active research (Remm et al., 2001; Datta et al., 2009).
evidence: This discusses challenges for extending the approach, with citations to relevant work.

claim: Protocols for generating paired sequence alignments more generally are an important area for development in this area.
source: Protocols for generating paired sequence alignments more generally are an important area for development in this area.
evidence: This is a statement about future research directions.

claim: Multiple sequence alignments were generated for each of the 4303 E. coli protein genes as identified by EcoGene 3.0 using HHblits and HHfilter.
source: Multiple sequence alignments were generated for each of the 4303 E. coli protein genes as identified by EcoGene 3.0 (Zhou et al., 2013) using HHblits (-n 8 -e 1E-20 -maxfilt ∞ -neffmax 20 -nodiff -realign_max ∞), and HHfilter (-id 100 -cov 75) in the HHsuite (version: 2.0.15, Remmert et al., 2011).
evidence: This describes the methods used for alignment generation.

claim: The alignment generation procedure resulted in 2340 non-redundant gene clusters.
source: This procedure resulted in 2340 non-redundant gene clusters.
evidence: This describes the outcome of the clustering procedure.

claim: GREMLIN constructs a global statistical model of the paired alignment, assigning a probability to every amino-acid sequence in the paired alignment.
source: GREMLIN constructs a global statistical model of the paired alignment, assigning a probability to every amino-acid sequence in the paired alignment
evidence: This describes the GREMLIN method.

claim: The GREMLIN model parameters are obtained by maximizing the regularized pseudo-likelihood of the alignment.
source: These parameters are obtained from the aligned sequences by maximizing the regularized pseudo-likelihood (Balakrishnan et al., 2011) of the alignment as described in (Kamisetty et al., 2013)
evidence: This describes the GREMLIN method, with citations to prior work.

claim: Previous approaches estimated parameters using an approximate moment matching approach by inverting a generalized covariance matrix.
source: Previous approaches (Morcos et al., 2011; Jones et al., 2012) estimated v, w using an approximate moment matching approach (Kamisetty et al., 2013) by inverting a generalized covariance matrix.
evidence: This describes prior methods, with citations.

claim: Previous approaches rely on a Gaussian-like approximation to the global partition function.
source: These rely on a Gaussian-like approximation to the global partition function.
evidence: This describes a characteristic of prior methods.

claim: Estimation via the pseudo-likelihood avoids the Gaussian-like approximation relying instead on local partition functions.
source: Unlike these approaches, estimation via the pseudo-likelihood avoids this approximation relying instead on local partition functions (Balakrishnan et al., 2011; Ekeberg et al., 2013; Kamisetty et al., 2013).
evidence: This describes an advantage of the pseudo-likelihood approach, with citations.

claim: The resulting global optimization problem can be efficiently solved using standard convex optimization techniques.
source: The resulting global optimization problem can be efficiently solved using standard convex optimization techniques and provides estimates for each vector vi and matrix wij (Kamisetty et al., 2013).
evidence: This describes the computational approach, with citation.

claim: The study only considers gene pairs with conserved intergenic distances in 60% of genomes and with fewer than 20 annotated genes between them.
source: Defining Δgene as the number of annotated genes between a gene pair, we only consider pairs with Δgene conserved in 60% of genomes and less than 20.
evidence: This describes the criteria for selecting gene pairs.

claim: A sigmoidal function of the coupling strength and the number of sequences per position in the complex accurately fits the observed contact frequency data.
source: A sigmoidal function of the coupling strength and the number of sequences per position in the complex accurately fits the observed contact frequency data ('Materials and methods' and Figure 1—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This describes the fitting of a model to the data, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Residue pairs within 8 Å in the TRAP complex model are connected by yellow bars in Figure 5.
source: Residue pairs with GREMLIN scores ≥ 0.60 are connected by yellow bars; the structures are pulled apart for clarity.
evidence: This describes the visualization in Figure 5.

claim: The bacterial 50S ribosomal subunit is the largest evolutionarily conserved bacterial multiprotein complex with an atomic resolution structure.
source: We began by studying residue–residue coupling parameters in the bacterial 50S ribosomal subunit—the largest evolutionarily conserved bacterial multiprotein complex with an atomic resolution structure.
evidence: This is a statement about the 50S ribosome used to justify its selection for study.
